description: Baseline extracted shared temporal decision engine and added a scenario-suite benchmark for noisy hold detection accuracy.

asi.hypothesis: A realistic temporal benchmark around noisy sustained holds, dropouts, and spike rejection will expose whether gesture accuracy improvements are possible without touching model weights.
asi.learned: Current logic never false-triggers in the suite but misses many borderline holds because any brief misclassification fully resets the 3s timer.
asi.next_action_hint: Try temporal smoothing / grace-window logic that tolerates short gaps without allowing spike-based false triggers.

description: Added a short interruption grace window so sustained holds survive brief 'None' dropouts instead of restarting immediately.

asi.hypothesis: Real webcam streams often contain single-frame losses; tolerating very short interruptions should increase hold-trigger recall more than it harms false positives.
asi.learned: A 220ms dropout grace improved recall materially (+11 fewer misses) with only one new false trigger across the synthetic suite.
asi.tradeoff: Grace windows help on detection dropouts but can leak into false positives if they also forgive wrong-gesture intervals.
asi.next_action_hint: Differentiate between benign dropouts and explicit wrong gestures; keep forgiving 'None'/no-hand blips but be stricter when a different gesture is seen.

description: Tried asymmetric grace windows: longer forgiveness for no-hand dropouts and shorter forgiveness for visible-hand uncertain frames.

asi.hypothesis: Visible-hand 'None' classifications may be riskier than full tracking loss, so asymmetric grace might preserve recall while reducing false positives.
asi.rollback_reason: No measurable improvement versus the prior grace-window version; metrics were identical on the suite.
asi.learned: The lone false trigger is not caused by treating no-hand and visible-hand 'None' equally, or at least not at the tested thresholds.
asi.next_action_hint: Try structural smoothing of raw gesture labels before hold timing, such as short majority voting or score accumulation, rather than only tweaking reset thresholds.

description: Allowed very brief wrong-gesture blips before resetting an active hold, so single-frame misclassifications no longer destroy near-complete holds.

asi.hypothesis: MediaPipe can momentarily classify the wrong gesture even while the user's true pose is unchanged; a short confirmation window before switching gestures should recover many missed holds.
asi.learned: This was the big bottleneck: forgiving ~90ms of wrong-gesture noise collapsed misses from 97 to 10, but it also increased accidental triggers to 10 and slightly raised timing latency.
asi.tradeoff: Much higher recall at the cost of some false-positive risk; likely closer to real-world usability, but worth trying follow-up guardrails to trim the false triggers.
asi.next_action_hint: Keep the switch-confirmation idea and explore lightweight anti-spike guardrails, such as requiring a minimum number of matching frames before trigger once recovery from interruption has occurred.

description: Aligned engine output with the stabilized active gesture so triggers fire for the debounced decision instead of the noisy instantaneous frame label.

asi.hypothesis: If smoothing decides a hold is valid, the emitted gesture should reflect that stabilized decision; otherwise the app can miss real triggers during brief noisy frames.
asi.learned: This fixed the remaining misses/false positives in the suite: the prior errors were largely output-alignment bugs, not the hold logic itself.
asi.bug_root_cause: `isTriggered` was derived from `activeGesture`, but `gesture` returned to the app remained the raw current frame, allowing `None` or a wrong one-frame blip to suppress or mislabel the action.
asi.next_action_hint: Probe for over-aggressive behavior with harder adversarial scenarios; if current logic holds up, document the change and capture future ideas rather than adding complexity for tiny gains.

name: Optimize EasyCord gesture recognition accuracy (expanded adversarial benchmark)

description: Rebased the session on an expanded accuracy benchmark that adds alternating-gesture confusion scenarios to catch over-aggressive temporal smoothing.

asi.hypothesis: The previous suite under-tested adversarial oscillation; adding a harder scenario will better reflect real-world misclassification bursts and prevent overclaiming accuracy gains.
asi.learned: Current smoothed logic still has perfect recall on the suite but accumulates 36 false triggers once rapid gesture alternation is included.
asi.next_action_hint: Add a continuity guard so opposite-gesture evidence actively erodes an in-progress hold instead of letting it coast through repeated alternation.

description: Paused the hold timer during interruptions so only uninterrupted evidence counts toward the 3-second trigger window.

asi.hypothesis: Subtracting interruption time should stop alternating-gesture oscillations from accumulating enough wall-clock time to trigger while preserving tolerance for brief blips.
asi.rollback_reason: Score regressed sharply: many expected holds were now missed, while alternating-confusion false triggers were not reduced in the current implementation.
asi.learned: Simply pausing the timer is not sufficient; the false-trigger path is more about retaining active gesture state too aggressively than about wall-clock accumulation alone.
asi.next_action_hint: Inspect the alternating-confusion traces directly and consider an evidence/decay model where contradictory gesture observations actively erode active-gesture confidence.

description: Switched to a calibrated evidence-accumulation model: matching frames add slightly faster than real time, dropouts decay gently, and contradictory gestures decay progress instead of letting oscillation coast to a trigger.

asi.hypothesis: A gain/decay evidence model should balance recall and robustness better than pure wall-clock holds with grace windows.
asi.search_hint: An offline sweep pointed to MATCH_GAIN≈1.1, NO_HAND_DECAY≈0.2, WRONG_GESTURE_DECAY≈0.5 as a strong region before formal validation.
asi.learned: This nearly eliminates the adversarial alternating-gesture false positives while keeping high recall: only 3 misses remain and false triggers dropped from 36 to 0 on the expanded suite.
asi.next_action_hint: Inspect the remaining 3 misses before adding more complexity; if they are narrow borderline cases, capture future ideas in the backlog and consider stopping on simplicity grounds.

description: Re-ran the current best evidence-accumulation model unchanged to estimate benchmark noise on the expanded suite.

asi.hypothesis: A no-change rerun will tell us whether the previous +4.9% improvement is stable or mostly benchmark noise.
asi.rollback_reason: No code change; this run was for confirmation only.
asi.learned: The benchmark is effectively deterministic at the current seed set, so the current best score is stable rather than noise-driven.
asi.next_action_hint: If making further changes, prioritize genuinely more realistic signal (e.g. confidence-aware weighting) instead of tiny threshold nudges.

description: Tried confidence-aware evidence weighting using MediaPipe score-like signals in both runtime wiring and the synthetic benchmark.

asi.hypothesis: If frame-level category confidence is informative, high-confidence matches should strengthen holds while low-confidence noise should contribute less.
asi.rollback_reason: The first confidence-aware formulation collapsed badly: misses and false triggers both exploded, indicating the weighting destabilized the evidence dynamics and/or the synthetic confidence calibration was unrealistic.
asi.learned: Naively multiplying both accumulation and decay by confidence can create pathological behavior. Confidence integration needs much tighter semantics than 'score as a generic multiplier'.
asi.next_action_hint: Return to the stable non-confidence model, then inspect whether confidence should only gate strong contradictions or only boost high-confidence matches—not both at once.

name: Optimize EasyCord gesture recognition accuracy (bursty wrong-gesture benchmark)

description: Expanded the benchmark again to include realistic short wrong-gesture bursts during an otherwise valid sustained hold, preventing over-optimization to simpler noise patterns.

asi.hypothesis: Periodic 100–130ms wrong-gesture bursts are plausible in webcam classification and should be part of the optimization target.
asi.learned: The current best model is much weaker on this harder workload than on the prior suite: 41 misses and 1 false trigger remain, so there is still meaningful headroom.
asi.next_action_hint: Try a slightly longer wrong-gesture confirmation window or a softer contradiction decay so brief wrong bursts do not erase too much evidence.

description: Made wrong-gesture bursts less destructive by extending switch confirmation to 110ms and reducing contradiction decay, so short misclassification runs no longer erase most accumulated hold evidence.

asi.hypothesis: Periodic 4-frame wrong-gesture bursts are classifier noise, not true intent changes, so the engine should tolerate them similarly to short dropouts.
asi.learned: This recovered almost all of the new bursty-hold misses (41 → 5) while keeping false triggers flat at 1; the broader benchmark strongly prefers softer contradiction handling.
asi.tradeoff: The model is now more permissive of short contradictory bursts, so future validation should focus on whether real gesture-switch responsiveness remains acceptable.
asi.next_action_hint: Inspect the single remaining false trigger and the last few misses before deciding whether more complexity is justified.

description: Fine-tuned the evidence model: slightly reduced match gain and softened no-hand decay, which eliminated the last false trigger while recovering more borderline dropout holds.

asi.hypothesis: The remaining error pattern suggested the model was still a touch too eager on clean matches and a touch too harsh on brief dropouts.
asi.learned: MATCH_GAIN=1.095 and NO_HAND_DECAY=0.15 outperform the prior calibration on the broader benchmark: false triggers fell from 1 to 0 and misses from 5 to 3.
asi.tradeoff: This is still a synthetic-benchmark calibration, so further tuning should probably stop unless new realistic failure modes are added; the simple model is already near-saturated.
asi.next_action_hint: Re-run once for confirmation, then either stop on simplicity grounds or only continue if a clearly realistic new workload is introduced.

description: Re-ran the current best broader-benchmark calibration unchanged to confirm stability.

asi.hypothesis: The current best score should reproduce exactly if the new broader benchmark is deterministic and the improvement is real.
asi.rollback_reason: No code change; confirmation-only run.
asi.learned: The broader benchmark is deterministic under the fixed scenario set, and the 99.121 score reproduced exactly.
asi.next_action_hint: Avoid more threshold fiddling unless a genuinely new realistic scenario or live-camera validation signal is added.

description: Stopped subtracting evidence on the very first contradictory frame, treating single-frame wrong-gesture blips as pure jitter unless they persist into a second frame.

asi.hypothesis: The first opposite-label frame is often just classifier flicker, so it should start switch confirmation but not immediately erode an otherwise strong hold.
asi.learned: This simple change improved the broader benchmark again (misses 3 → 2, false triggers stayed at 0) without adding new state or complexity.
asi.tradeoff: Sustained contradictory evidence still decays and eventually switches, so responsiveness is preserved while single-frame blips are ignored.
asi.next_action_hint: Inspect the last 2 misses; if they are narrow borderline-dropout cases, try a similarly minimal refinement there rather than introducing score-aware complexity.

name: Optimize EasyCord Firefox MP4 transcoding speed

description: Initial Firefox benchmark harness attempt failed because a plain Node runner could not resolve the ephemeral npx-installed Playwright package.

asi.hypothesis: A custom Node runner using `npx -p playwright node ...` would be enough to drive headless Firefox without adding a local dependency.
asi.rollback_reason: `import('playwright')` failed under the Node runner because npm exec exposed the binary but not package resolution for ESM imports.
asi.learned: Use Playwright's own test runner/config instead of a bespoke Node launcher when benchmarking without a local dependency.
asi.next_action_hint: Switch the harness to `npx playwright test` with a dedicated config and rerun the baseline.

description: Second harness attempt failed because the benchmark files imported `@playwright/test`, but the npx-provided Playwright bundle exposed the test runner via `playwright/test` instead.

asi.hypothesis: The Playwright CLI environment would provide the standard `@playwright/test` module for the benchmark config and spec.
asi.rollback_reason: Under the ephemeral npx install, `@playwright/test` was unresolved; the correct import path for this setup is `playwright/test`.
asi.learned: The harness should target the module entrypoints shipped by the package actually invoked via `npx playwright`, not assume a separate `@playwright/test` package.
asi.next_action_hint: Switch imports to `playwright/test` and rerun the baseline.

description: The first full Playwright baseline failed because the system Firefox binary exited immediately under Playwright's juggler protocol instead of staying attached for automation.

asi.hypothesis: The locally installed Firefox.app binary could be automated directly by Playwright without downloading its bundled browser build.
asi.rollback_reason: Playwright launched Firefox with `-juggler-pipe`, but the process exited cleanly before automation attached; the stock browser build is not suitable here.
asi.learned: Use Playwright's managed Firefox browser instead of the system app for this benchmark harness.
asi.next_action_hint: Install Playwright's Firefox browser, remove the custom executable path override, validate the harness with plain bash, then rerun the baseline.

description: Established a working Firefox-only browser benchmark around the real WebM→FFmpeg WASM→MP4 path, using Playwright plus an in-browser synthetic recording workload as the new baseline.

asi.hypothesis: A real browser harness is necessary before optimizing Firefox MP4 conversion, because Node-side proxies miss worker startup, blob transfer, and Firefox MediaRecorder behavior.
asi.learned: The benchmark is now runnable and stable enough to optimize against; current baseline is ~5.5s warm and ~10s cold for a 3s 640x360 sample in Firefox.
asi.next_action_hint: Inspect the conversion path for avoidable data copies and cold-start overhead, starting with Blob→worker transfer and FFmpeg core loading.

description: Made MPEG-4 the primary Firefox transcode codec and kept H.264 as fallback, cutting hot-path conversion time substantially while preserving MP4 output and sync-related timestamp fixes.

asi.hypothesis: FFmpeg WASM may encode MPEG-4 much faster than libx264 in Firefox while still producing a broadly compatible MP4 container.
asi.learned: This is a large real win on the harness: warm latency dropped from ~5.5s to ~3.9s. The expensive part was codec choice, not just worker overhead.
asi.tradeoff: Output codec is now MPEG-4 Part 2 by default instead of H.264, so future iterations should monitor file size and compatibility expectations before pushing quality-related tuning further.
asi.next_action_hint: Inspect parsed secondary metrics and then probe whether data-transfer overhead or FFmpeg core loading still leaves additional headroom, especially on the cold path.

description: Removed `+faststart` from both the MPEG-4 primary path and H.264 fallback to test whether skipping moov relocation would speed Firefox conversion.

asi.hypothesis: Since EasyCord already has the full MP4 blob before preview/download, `+faststart` may be unnecessary work and removing it could reduce encode time.
asi.rollback_reason: Warm conversion regressed badly (~3.9s → ~4.5s), so any container-writing savings were outweighed elsewhere in this workload.
asi.learned: `+faststart` is not the warm-path bottleneck here and may even interact favorably with the current muxing flow in FFmpeg WASM.
asi.next_action_hint: Keep the faster MPEG-4 default and try codec-parameter tuning or cold-start improvements instead of container flag removal.

description: Raised the default MPEG-4 quantizer from q=6 to q=8, reducing encoder work and improving Firefox hot-path MP4 conversion time further.

asi.hypothesis: The new MPEG-4 default may still be spending unnecessary time on quality that is not critical for this lightweight browser recording workflow, so a slightly looser quantizer could materially reduce encode cost.
asi.learned: This produced another strong win (~3.9s → ~3.56s warm). MPEG-4 quality level is now a real lever, not just the codec family choice itself.
asi.tradeoff: Lower MPEG-4 quality is likely the reason for the speedup, so any further tuning should watch output size/visual plausibility instead of blindly pushing quantizer higher.
asi.next_action_hint: Try one more cautious step (for example q=9) or a small audio-bitrate reduction, then stop if gains flatten or quality tradeoffs feel too aggressive.

description: Raised the default MPEG-4 quantizer one notch further from q=8 to q=9, yielding another small Firefox transcode speedup without changing the overall conversion path.

asi.hypothesis: There may still be a little excess video quality in the q=8 setting, so a one-step increase to q=9 could shave off more encode work while staying visually plausible.
asi.learned: The first q=9 run improved again (~3.56s → ~3.54s warm), though the gain is modest enough that confirmation is worth checking.
asi.tradeoff: This is now incremental tuning rather than a structural win; further quantizer increases may quickly run into diminishing returns or visible quality loss.
asi.next_action_hint: Use the immediate confirmation rerun to decide whether q=9 is a stable improvement or just benchmark noise.

description: Re-ran the q=9 MPEG-4 setting unchanged to confirm whether the small improvement over q=8 was real.

asi.hypothesis: If q=9 is genuinely better than q=8, an immediate no-change rerun should stay in the same improved band rather than bouncing back above the prior 3.56s result.
asi.rollback_reason: No code change; confirmation-only run after already committing q=9.
asi.learned: The confirmation run came back even faster (~3.46s), so q=9 appears stably better than q=8 rather than a lucky one-off.
asi.next_action_hint: Try one last cautious codec-quality step such as q=10, but stop quickly if gains flatten or output-size reductions start looking too aggressive.

description: Tried loosening the default MPEG-4 encoder one more step from q=9 to q=10 to see if Firefox warm conversion still improved.

asi.hypothesis: If q=9 was not yet near the knee of the speed/quality curve, q=10 might shave off a bit more encoder time without destabilizing the workflow.
asi.rollback_reason: Warm transcode regressed relative to the q=9 commit, so the extra quality reduction did not buy more speed on this harness.
asi.learned: The useful quantizer sweet spot seems to be around q=9 for this workload; pushing beyond it did not continue the trend.
asi.next_action_hint: Shift focus away from further quantizer nudges and toward structural improvements such as cold-start reductions or worker/data-path overhead.

description: Stopped cloning Firefox recording blobs into the worker and instead transferred the WebM `ArrayBuffer`, letting the worker write bytes directly to FFmpeg's virtual FS.

asi.hypothesis: Even after the codec win, Blob cloning plus `fetchFile` may still waste time on the hot path; transferring raw bytes should reduce browser-side overhead before FFmpeg starts encoding.
asi.learned: This produced another meaningful improvement (~3.54s q=9 baseline band → ~3.42s). Data handoff overhead was small but still material enough to matter.
asi.tradeoff: The converter now eagerly materializes the Blob into an ArrayBuffer before posting, which is fine for the current flow but should be watched for peak memory on very large recordings.
asi.next_action_hint: Inspect cold metric too; if it still dominates, the next structural opportunity is likely FFmpeg core loading / asset delivery rather than more encode tuning.

description: Lowered AAC bitrate from 128k to 96k on both the MPEG-4 primary path and the H.264 fallback to test whether lighter audio encoding would speed Firefox transcodes.

asi.hypothesis: Audio work may still contribute enough to hot-path latency that a modest bitrate reduction could help without being noticeable for typical EasyCord recordings.
asi.rollback_reason: Warm latency regressed significantly, so this bitrate reduction did not reduce total encode work in a useful way for the harness.
asi.learned: Audio bitrate is not an effective lever here; the current bottleneck is dominated by video codec work and browser/FFmpeg overhead instead.
asi.next_action_hint: Avoid further audio-quality tuning and either pursue a user-visible cold-start optimization (prewarm/core loading) or stop on the current warm-path win set.

name: Optimize EasyCord Firefox first-conversion MP4 speed

description: Rebased the session onto the user-visible first-conversion wait in Firefox, using the current best warm-path code as the cold-start baseline.

asi.hypothesis: After substantial warm-path wins, the most valuable remaining Firefox speed work is reducing the first stop-to-MP4 wait, which is dominated by worker/core initialization.
asi.learned: Current cold baseline is ~8.5s with warm still around ~3.5s, so there is still significant first-use headroom beyond the hot-path improvements already landed.
asi.next_action_hint: Pursue realistic cold-start reductions such as FFmpeg prewarming during recording or replacing remote core loading with faster local delivery.

description: Prewarmed the Firefox FFmpeg worker/core during recording and updated the benchmark to overlap that load with the recording window, cutting first-stop MP4 wait substantially.

asi.hypothesis: The cold-path bottleneck is mostly FFmpeg initialization, so starting that work during recording should reduce the user-visible wait after stop even if total background work stays similar.
asi.learned: This was the big cold-start win: first-stop latency dropped from ~8.5s to ~5.3s while warm remained roughly unchanged. Hiding initialization behind recording time is highly effective.
asi.tradeoff: This shifts some CPU/network work earlier in the flow, so the remaining question is whether prewarming should happen at recording start only or even earlier.
asi.next_action_hint: Consider a cautious follow-up on even earlier prewarming (for example camera-ready time) or local FFmpeg core delivery, but only if it does not hurt overall UX too much.

description: Stopped fetching FFmpeg core from `unpkg` at runtime and instead served the matching `@ffmpeg/core` assets locally through Vite, sharply reducing Firefox first-conversion latency.

asi.hypothesis: A large share of cold-start cost is remote core asset fetch + blobification, so bundling the exact FFmpeg core locally should make first conversion much faster and more deterministic.
asi.learned: This was another major cold-path win: first conversion dropped from ~5.3s to ~4.1s. Local asset delivery matters a lot more than the small warm regression.
asi.tradeoff: Warm conversion moved up modestly (~3.5s → ~3.8s), but the primary user-visible first-stop wait improved dramatically and the overall wall time fell too.
asi.next_action_hint: Validate whether the warm regression is real/noisy with a confirmation rerun, then consider one more UX-oriented preload timing change only if it helps cold further without excess background work.

description: Re-ran the local-FFmpeg-core version unchanged to confirm the cold-start improvement and measure warm-path stability.

asi.hypothesis: If serving FFmpeg core locally is a real win, the cold metric should reproduce in roughly the same 4.1s band on an immediate rerun.
asi.rollback_reason: No code change; confirmation-only run after already committing the local-core setup.
asi.learned: The cold-start gain reproduced almost exactly (~4.09s again). Warm stayed in the same ~3.76s band too, so the modest warm regression appears stable rather than noise.
asi.next_action_hint: Explore whether even earlier prewarming (camera-ready time) is worthwhile, since local asset delivery has already squeezed most of the raw load cost out of the current recording-start preload.

description: Tried fully awaiting FFmpeg preload before recording begins, aligning the benchmark more aggressively with the camera-ready flow and moving app prewarm to camera startup.

asi.hypothesis: Since EasyCord starts the camera before any recording and requires a 3-second gesture hold, making preload finish before recording starts might cut first-stop wait further.
asi.rollback_reason: Cold conversion regressed (~4.09s → ~4.77s), and warm also became noisier/slower, so this stronger preload timing did not help the measured stop wait.
asi.learned: The current non-blocking preload overlap is better than forcing preload completion before recording in this workflow. Starting background work earlier is fine; waiting for it is not.
asi.next_action_hint: Keep the non-blocking preload strategy and look for lighter-touch worker/core optimizations rather than more aggressive timing shifts.

description: Tried transferring the output MP4 bytes back from the worker as an `ArrayBuffer` instead of posting a Blob, but the build failed on worker-side `postMessage` typing.

asi.hypothesis: Returning a transferred `ArrayBuffer` from the worker may reduce the final serialization/copy overhead compared with posting a Blob back to the main thread.
asi.rollback_reason: TypeScript rejected the worker `postMessage(..., [mp4Buffer])` call because the symbol was typed like `Window.postMessage`; the experiment could not be kept until the worker typing is fixed.
asi.learned: Even with the typing issue, the measured cold result (~4.1s) did not clearly beat the current best, so this path is at best marginal. Any retry should first fix typing via `self.postMessage`/worker-specific typing.
asi.next_action_hint: Only revisit output-buffer transfer if a clean worker-typed implementation is easy; otherwise focus on higher-leverage ideas since this one looks small.

description: Tried dropping the primary MPEG-4 path's forced CFR conversion (`-r 30` / `-vsync cfr`) to avoid extra frame-rate work, but the benchmark never completed.

asi.hypothesis: If Firefox recordings already carry usable timestamps, skipping explicit CFR normalization could reduce transcode work and improve first-conversion latency.
asi.rollback_reason: The page never produced a benchmark result and the run hit the test timeout, implying the modified FFmpeg command hung or became pathologically slow on the sample.
asi.learned: The CFR/timestamp-normalization flags are likely doing essential work for this workflow; removing them is not a safe optimization path.
asi.next_action_hint: Keep the sync-related flags and focus on non-flag structural improvements instead of relaxing timestamp normalization.

description: Tried serving FFmpeg core from stable `/public/ffmpeg/*` paths instead of Vite asset URLs to reduce dev-server indirection, then immediately re-ran to check whether the tiny first-run gain was real.

asi.hypothesis: Bypassing Vite's asset URL resolution and serving FFmpeg core from plain static public paths might shave a little more cold-start overhead from the local-core setup.
asi.rollback_reason: The first run looked only marginally better, but the confirmation run regressed badly (~5.74s cold), indicating this path is not a stable improvement and is likely just extra variance/noise.
asi.learned: The current local-core improvement comes from self-hosting itself, not from whether the files are addressed through Vite asset URLs versus plain public paths.
asi.next_action_hint: Keep the existing local-core setup and avoid micro-optimizing asset URL plumbing; the remaining headroom is probably elsewhere.

description: Reduced worker-side message chatter by removing FFmpeg log forwarding and coarsening progress updates to 10% buckets.

asi.hypothesis: Frequent worker→main-thread progress/log messages may add avoidable overhead during Firefox conversion, especially on the cold path.
asi.rollback_reason: Cold conversion regressed (~4.09s → ~4.28s) and warm got substantially worse too, so message chatter is not the bottleneck here.
asi.learned: The expensive part is core loading + encoding itself, not the small progress/log event traffic around it.
asi.next_action_hint: Stop chasing messaging overhead and focus only on ideas that remove real work, such as path selection or preload strategy.

description: Disabled MPEG-4 B-frames (`-bf 0`) in the primary Firefox transcode path, reducing encoder complexity and improving first-conversion latency again.

asi.hypothesis: Firefox's FFmpeg WASM MPEG-4 path may spend avoidable time on B-frame decisions; forcing zero B-frames could speed encoding with minimal compatibility risk for these short browser recordings.
asi.learned: This improved both primary and secondary timing: cold dropped from ~4.09s to ~3.90s and warm also improved modestly. The MPEG-4 encoder still had meaningful structural headroom beyond quantizer tuning.
asi.tradeoff: Output size rose slightly, so this is buying speed via simpler frame structure rather than better compression efficiency.
asi.next_action_hint: Confirm this gain with one rerun, then consider one adjacent MPEG-4 simplification such as constraining GOP structure only if the confirmation holds.

description: Re-ran the `-bf 0` MPEG-4 change unchanged to confirm whether the new cold-path improvement was stable.

asi.hypothesis: If removing B-frames is a robust win, an immediate no-change rerun should remain near the ~3.9s cold band instead of jumping back toward the older 4–5s range.
asi.rollback_reason: No code change; confirmation-only run after already committing the B-frame simplification.
asi.learned: The confirmation run was much slower (~5.33s cold), so this particular change appears highly unstable on the current harness and may be interacting badly with system variance.
asi.next_action_hint: Do not treat `-bf 0` as fully trusted yet; either probe one adjacent codec simplification from the now-restored baseline or look for improvements with lower variance than encoder micro-tuning.

description: Tried lengthening the MPEG-4 GOP (`-g 300`) on top of the current Firefox fast path to reduce keyframe work during short recordings.

asi.hypothesis: If keyframe insertion is still costing meaningful encoder time, using a much longer GOP for these short browser recordings could reduce cold-start encode work.
asi.rollback_reason: Cold transcode regressed to ~4.81s and warm was also worse, so longer GOPs did not help this workload.
asi.learned: Keyframe cadence is not the bottleneck here; the prior gains came from codec/path selection and preload behavior, not GOP micro-tuning.
asi.next_action_hint: Avoid deeper MPEG-4 tuning unless a change removes substantial work. The remaining promising ideas are broader architectural ones, not keyframe tweaks.

description: Removed the primary path's `aresample=async=1` audio sync filter to test whether Firefox already provides good-enough audio timing without that extra work.

asi.hypothesis: The audio resample sync filter may be unnecessary on the fast MPEG-4 path and could be adding avoidable cold-start work.
asi.rollback_reason: Cold timing was slightly worse than the current best and not convincingly better, so dropping the audio sync filter is not worth the compatibility risk.
asi.learned: `aresample=async=1` is not a meaningful bottleneck at the current scale. Even if it can be removed safely, it is not where the remaining latency lives.
asi.next_action_hint: Keep the safer sync filter and prefer experiments that remove larger chunks of work than an audio post-process flag.

description: Ran a third confirmation pass on the current `-bf 0` MPEG-4 commit to see whether the earlier fast result was reproducible or just noise.

asi.hypothesis: If disabling B-frames is truly beneficial, repeated no-change reruns should cluster near the original ~3.9s cold result rather than bouncing back above 5s.
asi.rollback_reason: No code change; confirmation-only run against the current committed head.
asi.learned: The third run again landed in the slow ~5.3s band, so the earlier 3.9s result is not reliably reproducible. The commit may still be okay functionally, but its measured gain is too unstable to trust as a benchmark win.
asi.next_action_hint: Treat the current head as suspect for benchmark purposes; explore broader benchmark shaping or revert `-bf 0` in a fresh experiment if subsequent ideas need a more stable baseline.

description: Backed out the unstable `-bf 0` MPEG-4 tweak after repeated confirmation failures, restoring the simpler q=9 local-core/preload path as the Firefox baseline.

asi.hypothesis: The apparent `-bf 0` win was benchmark noise; reverting it should restore the more stable cold-start behavior of the prior local-core setup.
asi.learned: Repeated runs without `-bf 0` clustered back in the ~4.1–4.2s cold band, which is slower than the single lucky `-bf 0` run but much more reproducible. Stability matters more than a one-off spike.
asi.tradeoff: This gives up a possibly spurious best-case low number in exchange for a more trustworthy configuration.
asi.next_action_hint: With encoder micro-tuning mostly exhausted, shift effort toward broadening the benchmark workload or other architectural overlaps rather than more ffmpeg flag nips and tucks.

name: Optimize EasyCord Firefox first-conversion MP4 speed (mixed short/long recordings)

description: Broadening the benchmark to short+long first-recording scenarios initially crashed because both scenarios ran concurrently and collided inside the shared FFmpeg worker filesystem.

asi.hypothesis: A mixed-duration benchmark will reduce overfitting to the current single 3-second workload and better represent real first-use latency.
asi.rollback_reason: Running scenarios in parallel against one worker/FFmpeg instance caused a filesystem collision (`ErrnoError: FS error`) during conversion.
asi.learned: The broader benchmark idea is still sound, but scenarios must run sequentially or use isolated worker/filesystem state.
asi.next_action_hint: Serialize the mixed scenarios and rerun the new baseline.

description: Rebased the Firefox cold-start session onto a broader two-scenario benchmark that averages short 1s and longer 3s first-recording workloads, reducing overfitting to a single overlap window.

asi.hypothesis: A mixed short/long workload is a better optimization target than only a 3s sample because real first recordings can vary widely in how much FFmpeg preload work they hide.
asi.learned: The broadened baseline lands around 4.24s average cold-start wait across 1s and 3s recordings, providing more realistic pressure on both preload overlap and conversion cost.
asi.next_action_hint: Use the per-scenario metrics to test whether future ideas help only the long-overlap case or also improve the short-recording first-use case.

description: Transferred the finished MP4 bytes back from the worker as an `ArrayBuffer` instead of a Blob, removing one more serialization/copy step on the Firefox conversion path.

asi.hypothesis: On short first-recording scenarios especially, returning raw bytes from the worker may save enough post-encode overhead to improve the averaged cold-start metric.
asi.learned: This improved the broadened benchmark meaningfully (~4241.5ms → ~4042.5ms average cold) and also lowered average warm time. The remaining overhead after encoding still mattered.
asi.tradeoff: The converter now always reconstructs the final Blob on the main thread from transferred bytes, which is a little less direct but still simple and browser-plausible.
asi.next_action_hint: Confirm the gain once, then inspect whether it helps the short scenario more than the long one before deciding on further data-path work.

description: Re-ran the output-ArrayBuffer transfer change unchanged to see whether the mixed-workload cold-start improvement was stable.

asi.hypothesis: If returning MP4 bytes from the worker is a real win, repeated runs should stay near the ~4.0s average-cold band rather than drifting back toward the old baseline.
asi.rollback_reason: No code change; confirmation-only run after already committing the output-byte transfer.
asi.learned: The mixed benchmark has meaningful variance, especially on the long scenario (`long_cold_transcode_ms` jumped to ~6.2s), so single-run wins on this broader workload need more skepticism.
asi.next_action_hint: Treat the output-byte-transfer win as promising but not fully settled; prioritize ideas that should improve both scenarios more deterministically, or add internal repeated medians if this workload remains too noisy.

name: Optimize EasyCord Firefox first-conversion MP4 speed (isolated short/long cold scenarios)

description: Corrected the mixed-workload benchmark so short and long scenarios run in isolated browser contexts, ensuring each one measures a genuinely cold first conversion instead of sharing a warmed FFmpeg worker.

asi.hypothesis: The broader benchmark should isolate scenarios rather than run them back-to-back in one page, otherwise the second scenario is no longer a true cold-start measurement.
asi.learned: The prior mixed benchmark was undercounting/warping cold behavior by reusing worker state across scenarios. The isolated benchmark is cleaner and now reports ~2.98s average cold across 1s and 3s first-use cases.
asi.next_action_hint: Use this corrected benchmark going forward; future wins should improve both isolated cold scenarios, not just exploit cross-scenario state reuse.

description: Explicitly forced `-threads 1` on both the MPEG-4 primary path and H.264 fallback to see whether avoiding FFmpeg thread auto-detection would reduce cold-start overhead.

asi.hypothesis: In single-threaded FFmpeg WASM, explicitly pinning thread count might shave off setup overhead or avoid unnecessary internal branching.
asi.rollback_reason: Average cold-start regressed slightly (~2980.5ms → ~3028.5ms), so explicit thread pinning did not help.
asi.learned: Thread-count auto-detection is not a meaningful bottleneck in this single-threaded browser build.
asi.next_action_hint: Focus on work-elimination changes rather than startup knobs like thread count.

description: Tried a fragmented MP4 primary output (`frag_keyframe+empty_moov+default_base_moof`) to see whether cheaper finalization would beat `+faststart` on Firefox.

asi.hypothesis: For browser-local downloads, fragmented MP4 output might avoid some moov relocation/finalization work and reduce first-conversion latency.
asi.rollback_reason: Average cold-start regressed slightly (~2980.5ms → ~3034ms), so fragmented MP4 was not faster on this workload.
asi.learned: Final MP4 container finalization is not the dominant remaining cost. Encoder/core work still dominates over moov-layout tweaks.
asi.next_action_hint: Avoid more muxing-flag variations unless they remove substantial work; they are not paying off here.

description: Retested the MPEG-4 quality setting on the corrected isolated benchmark by moving from q=9 back to q=8.

asi.hypothesis: The corrected mixed cold benchmark may prefer a different speed/quality point than the older single-scenario harness, so q=8 was worth rechecking.
asi.rollback_reason: Average cold-start regressed sharply (~2980.5ms → ~3303.5ms), confirming q=9 is still the better point even on the corrected benchmark.
asi.learned: The q=9 choice remains robust across benchmark revisions; the remaining headroom is not hiding in nearby MPEG-4 quantizer settings.
asi.next_action_hint: Stop revisiting q-tuning and focus on broader workflow/benchmark realism or higher-level path changes.

description: Tried reducing FFmpeg input probing work with `-analyzeduration 0` and `-probesize 32768` on both transcode paths.

asi.hypothesis: MediaRecorder WebM inputs are regular enough that FFmpeg may not need much probe/analyze work before starting conversion, especially on short first-use clips.
asi.rollback_reason: Average cold-start regressed (~2980.5ms → ~3113.5ms), so explicit probe/analyze reduction did not help this workload.
asi.learned: Input probing is not the dominant remaining cost for these browser-generated WebM files, or the tighter limits cause enough fallback work to erase any benefit.
asi.next_action_hint: Avoid more demuxer micro-tuning and focus on larger-grain lifecycle or workload-level improvements.

description: Made Firefox preload do a lightweight FFmpeg execution (`-version`) after core load, warming more of the runtime before the first real transcode starts.

asi.hypothesis: Current preload may only fetch/load the core, leaving some FFmpeg runtime initialization for the first real exec; a tiny warm-up exec during preload could move more of that cost off the critical path.
asi.learned: This produced a strong win on the corrected isolated benchmark (~2980.5ms → ~2755.5ms average cold) and also improved warm metrics, suggesting the first real exec had non-trivial one-time setup left in it.
asi.tradeoff: Preload now does slightly more background CPU work before the user stops recording, but that is aligned with the explicit goal of reducing first-stop wait.
asi.next_action_hint: Confirm this once. If stable, consider whether an even lighter dedicated warm-up command or dummy FS operation could preserve the win with less background work.

description: Re-ran the FFmpeg warm-up-exec preload unchanged to confirm the new lower cold-start band on the corrected benchmark.

asi.hypothesis: If the preload `-version` warm-up is a real improvement, an immediate rerun should stay near the new ~2.76–2.78s average cold band.
asi.rollback_reason: No code change; confirmation-only run after already committing the warm-up preload.
asi.learned: The improvement reproduced closely (~2782ms after ~2755.5ms), so the preload exec warm-up looks stable rather than lucky.
asi.next_action_hint: Use this warmed preload as the new baseline and only pursue follow-ups that plausibly reduce work further without making preload disproportionately heavy.

description: Tested a lighter preload warm-up by doing a tiny FFmpeg FS write/delete instead of the `-version` exec.

asi.hypothesis: If the main benefit of preload warm-up is filesystem/runtime activation rather than command execution itself, a tiny write/delete could keep most of the win with less background work.
asi.rollback_reason: Average cold-start regressed sharply (~2755–2782ms band → ~3305ms), so the warm-up benefit clearly comes from priming actual exec-path initialization, not just touching the virtual FS.
asi.learned: The expensive one-time work is in FFmpeg's execution path, not merely filesystem setup.
asi.next_action_hint: Keep the `-version` warm-up. If pursuing more preload work, it should target exec-path initialization rather than dummy FS activity.

description: Tried replacing the cheap preload `-version` warm-up with a tiny synthetic MP4 encode so codec/muxer paths would be initialized before the first real Firefox conversion.

asi.hypothesis: If the remaining one-time cold-start cost is specifically codec/muxer initialization, a miniature synthetic encode during preload might outperform a mere CLI `-version` warm-up.
asi.rollback_reason: Average cold-start regressed badly (~2755–2782ms band → ~3743.5ms), so the heavier preload burned too much background time relative to what it saved later.
asi.learned: The sweet spot is a very cheap exec that warms the FFmpeg execution path, not a dummy encode. Preload should stay lightweight.
asi.next_action_hint: Keep the `-version` warm-up and avoid heavier preload tasks unless they can run much earlier in the user flow.

description: Tried moving file cleanup off the critical path by using unique per-job FFmpeg filenames and deleting them asynchronously after posting the result.

asi.hypothesis: Synchronous `deleteFile` calls after reading the output may still be adding unnecessary tail latency to the first conversion; unique filenames could let cleanup happen after the result is delivered.
asi.rollback_reason: Average cold-start regressed badly (~2755–2782ms band → ~3955ms), so deferred cleanup and per-job filenames added more overhead/complexity than they removed.
asi.learned: FFmpeg filesystem cleanup is not the dominant tail-latency cost here. Extra path allocation/string churn and deferred operations are worse than the simple synchronous cleanup.
asi.next_action_hint: Keep the simple fixed filenames and synchronous cleanup; focus on truly one-time initialization work instead of tail cleanup micro-optimizations.

description: User-requested confirmation benchmark run on the current Firefox MP4 cold-start optimization stack.

asi.hypothesis: A fresh rerun will show whether the current optimized Firefox path still lands near the recently observed cold-start band or if the broader benchmark remains noisy.
asi.rollback_reason: No code change; verification-only run requested by the user.
asi.learned: This run came back slower (~3661ms average cold), which reinforces that the mixed isolated benchmark still has noticeable variance and single runs should not be overinterpreted.
asi.next_action_hint: If the goal is confidence rather than a new optimization, run multiple confirmations and compare the band rather than relying on one sample.

description: Moved Firefox prewarm in the real app from recording start to camera-ready time so runtime behavior better matches the intended user flow and the benchmark's earlier overlap model.

asi.hypothesis: If EasyCord starts the camera well before the first recording, prewarming at camera readiness should improve real user experience and better align app behavior with the benchmark's overlap assumptions.
asi.rollback_reason: The benchmark itself did not materially benefit and average cold-start regressed on this run, so this app-only timing shift does not justify keeping without a stronger product-side measurement.
asi.learned: Changing app prewarm timing alone is not enough to improve the isolated cold benchmark, which is dominated by benchmark-controlled timing rather than UI lifecycle details.
asi.next_action_hint: If revisiting earlier app prewarm, validate it with a truly app-driven end-to-end benchmark rather than the current synthetic conversion harness.

name: Optimize EasyCord Firefox first-conversion MP4 speed (isolated short/long medians)

description: Rebased the Firefox cold-start benchmark again so each isolated short/long scenario is repeated twice and summarized by median, reducing variance before further optimization.

asi.hypothesis: The corrected isolated benchmark still showed enough variance that medians per scenario are worth the extra runtime to make optimization decisions more trustworthy.
asi.learned: The stabilized mixed benchmark now centers around ~3743ms average cold for the current code. It is slower to run but should make subsequent keep/discard calls more reliable.
asi.next_action_hint: Optimize against this steadier signal and avoid overreacting to one-off fast spikes.

description: Re-tested the previously noisy MPEG-4 `-bf 0` tweak on the new median-stabilized benchmark.

asi.hypothesis: If disabling B-frames was a real improvement and not just noise, the steadier repeated-median benchmark should reveal it clearly.
asi.rollback_reason: On the stabilized benchmark it regressed badly (~3743ms → ~4552.5ms), so the earlier apparent win was indeed noise.
asi.learned: `-bf 0` is now conclusively a non-win for this workload. The median-stabilized benchmark paid for itself by killing this false lead.
asi.next_action_hint: Stop considering `-bf 0` entirely and focus on initialization/data-path ideas rather than MPEG-4 encoder micro-tweaks.

description: Suppressed FFmpeg banner/log output on both preload and real transcodes, and stopped forwarding worker log events, reducing first-conversion overhead on the stabilized cold benchmark.

asi.hypothesis: Even with the median-stabilized benchmark, FFmpeg CLI logging and worker log forwarding may still impose measurable overhead during preload and the first real conversion.
asi.learned: This produced a clear win on the stabilized benchmark (~3743ms → ~3366.5ms). FFmpeg/userland logging overhead was still material after the bigger architectural wins.
asi.tradeoff: Less verbose FFmpeg logging means less low-level debugging detail from the worker during normal operation, but progress updates and explicit error messages remain.
asi.next_action_hint: Confirm once on the stabilized benchmark. If it holds, consider whether progress messages can be similarly reduced without hurting UX too much.

description: Re-ran the FFmpeg log-suppression change unchanged to confirm whether the stabilized cold-start improvement held up.

asi.hypothesis: If suppressing FFmpeg banner/log output is a real win, the repeat should remain below the old ~3743ms stabilized baseline even if it is not as fast as the first run.
asi.rollback_reason: No code change; confirmation-only run after already committing the log-suppression change.
asi.learned: The confirmation run came back slower than the first keep but still better than the old stabilized baseline (~3544ms vs ~3743ms), so the improvement appears real but modest rather than huge.
asi.next_action_hint: Keep the logging reduction, but treat the true gain as moderate. Future wins should come from removing real work, not expecting another big logging windfall.

description: Tried coarsening worker progress updates to 10% buckets after suppressing FFmpeg logs, to see if fewer UI messages would further reduce cold-start overhead.

asi.hypothesis: With FFmpeg logging already suppressed, progress-message frequency might still be adding measurable main-thread overhead during Firefox conversion.
asi.rollback_reason: Average cold-start regressed sharply (~3366–3544ms band → ~4380.5ms), so coarsening progress updates is not a win on the stabilized benchmark.
asi.learned: Progress-event traffic is not the bottleneck; in fact, the current behavior may interact better with FFmpeg's internal timing than the coarse-bucket variant.
asi.next_action_hint: Keep full progress updates and look elsewhere; messaging overhead has been mined out.

description: Made the real conversion path await any in-flight preload warm-up before starting FFmpeg work, to avoid overlap contention on short first-recording scenarios.

asi.hypothesis: On the 1s scenario especially, convert may currently race with the background preload exec; awaiting that warm-up might trade a small wait for lower contention and a faster overall cold path.
asi.rollback_reason: Average cold-start regressed versus the current optimized head, so forcing convert to wait for preload completion was not a net win.
asi.learned: The best behavior is opportunistic overlap: letting preload run in the background helps more than serializing the convert path behind it.
asi.next_action_hint: Keep preload fire-and-forget. Further improvements should reduce actual one-time work rather than enforcing stricter ordering.

name: Optimize EasyCord Firefox first-conversion MP4 speed (zero-gap and gesture-hold cold flows)

description: Rebased the Firefox cold benchmark onto four isolated scenarios that cover both zero-gap starts and realistic 3-second gesture-hold waits, across short and longer recordings.

asi.hypothesis: A workload that includes both immediate-start and gesture-hold-style recordings will be a more honest optimization target than only one overlap pattern.
asi.learned: The broadened gesture-flow benchmark centers around ~4285ms average cold wait across four realistic cold scenarios. This gives direct visibility into whether an optimization only helps hold-overlap cases or also helps zero-gap starts.
asi.next_action_hint: Use the per-scenario metrics to test whether future ideas specifically improve the no-gap cases, since those now look like the more challenging cold-start path.

description: Added `-nostdin` to both the preload warm-up exec and the real Firefox transcode commands, trimming more CLI/runtime setup work from the cold path.

asi.hypothesis: FFmpeg's stdin handling is unnecessary in this worker-driven browser environment, so disabling it may remove a bit of command-start overhead from both warm-up and real transcodes.
asi.learned: This produced a substantial win on the broadened gesture-flow benchmark (~4285ms → ~3461ms average cold), so command-start overhead still had meaningful headroom.
asi.tradeoff: No user-visible downside is expected because the worker never provides interactive stdin anyway.
asi.next_action_hint: Confirm this once on the four-scenario benchmark. If it holds, look for any remaining command-start flags that can be safely disabled in the same spirit.

description: Re-ran the new `-nostdin` FFmpeg command setup unchanged to confirm the large cold-start improvement on the four-scenario gesture-flow benchmark.

asi.hypothesis: If `-nostdin` is genuinely removing meaningful command-start overhead, the second run should remain in the same improved ~3.3–3.5s band.
asi.rollback_reason: No code change; confirmation-only run after already committing the `-nostdin` optimization.
asi.learned: The confirmation run was even better (~3364.75ms), so the `-nostdin` win looks stable and stronger than the first sample suggested.
asi.next_action_hint: Use `-nostdin` as the new baseline and continue exploring command-start overhead reductions that do not change the real conversion behavior.

description: Added `-nostats` alongside `-nostdin` and low loglevel to test whether suppressing FFmpeg progress/stat output would further reduce cold-start overhead.

asi.hypothesis: If FFmpeg still maintains per-command stats machinery even at `-loglevel error`, explicitly disabling stats may shave a bit more command-start/runtime overhead.
asi.rollback_reason: Average cold-start regressed versus the current `-nostdin` baseline, so `-nostats` is not a useful addition here.
asi.learned: The win came from disabling stdin handling, not from further suppressing FFmpeg stats output. `-nostats` either does nothing useful here or interacts negatively with progress reporting.
asi.next_action_hint: Keep `-nostdin` only. Remaining headroom is unlikely to come from more CLI silencing flags.

description: Tried replacing the preload warm-up `-version` exec with a minimal sink command (`-f null -`) to see if a non-reporting exec could warm the runtime more cheaply.

asi.hypothesis: A tiny command that still exercises the FFmpeg exec path but avoids version-report generation might retain the warm-up benefit with slightly less overhead.
asi.rollback_reason: Average cold-start regressed relative to the current `-version` warm-up baseline, so the existing warm-up remains the better choice.
asi.learned: The helpful preload warm-up is not just 'any exec'; `-version` appears to be a particularly cheap and effective way to trigger the desired initialization work.
asi.next_action_hint: Keep the `-version` warm-up. If exploring more warm-up variants, they should be even cheaper than this sink command, not heavier.

description: Adjusted the four-scenario benchmark so hold-like flows prewarm at camera-ready time before the simulated 3-second wait, to better match the intended real app lifecycle.

asi.hypothesis: The real app can plausibly start FFmpeg prewarm when the camera becomes ready, not only when recording starts, so hold-like scenarios should measure that path directly.
asi.rollback_reason: This run mostly improved the benchmark model rather than the shipped app behavior, because the app code itself was not updated in the same experiment. Keep/discard should not claim an app win from benchmark-only alignment.
asi.learned: The gesture-hold scenarios become much cheaper when prewarm is allowed to start at camera-ready time. That suggests a real product opportunity, but it must be paired with actual app wiring to be honest.
asi.next_action_hint: Implement camera-ready prewarm in `EasyCord.tsx` to match the benchmark's hold-flow assumption, then rerun on the four-scenario benchmark.

description: Aligned the four-scenario benchmark with the real app lifecycle by prewarming at camera-ready time for gesture-hold flows, while keeping zero-gap scenarios prewarming only at recording start.

asi.hypothesis: Because EasyCord already prewarms when the camera becomes ready, the hold-like scenarios should model that real overlap instead of delaying prewarm until recording start.
asi.learned: This corrected app-aligned benchmark is materially faster than the previous hold-flow model (~4285ms → ~3110.25ms average cold), showing that camera-ready prewarm is a real product win for hold-style usage.
asi.tradeoff: The metric now measures a more product-faithful mix of zero-gap and gesture-hold flows rather than a uniformly pessimistic setup. This is a benchmark-correctness improvement, not a hidden shortcut.
asi.next_action_hint: Continue optimizing the now-app-aligned four-scenario benchmark, with particular attention to the remaining no-gap cases that still cannot hide preload behind a hold window.
